overview.text: Sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) is a colorless, oily acid with major industrial importance. It is diprotic, meaning each molecule can donate two hydrogen ions in separate steps; the first ionization is nearly complete, while the second is less complete. In the contact process, sulfur is converted to sulfur dioxide, then to sulfur trioxide over a catalyst—often vanadium-based—and the trioxide is absorbed to make sulfuric acid. The acid is used to produce phosphate fertilizers and serves as the electrolyte in lead-acid batteries. Concentrated sulfuric acid is corrosive, and mixing it with water releases considerable heat.

key_facts.text: Sulfuric acid’s formula is H₂SO₄; it can donate two protons, but its second ionization is less complete than its first.
In the contact process, sulfur dioxide is catalytically oxidized to sulfur trioxide, which is absorbed to produce sulfuric acid; vanadium-based catalysts are commonly used.
A major use is making phosphate fertilizers; sulfuric acid is also used in lead-acid batteries.
In a lead-acid battery, sulfuric acid solution is the electrolyte. During discharge, it reacts with the electrodes to form lead sulfate and water.
Sulfuric acid is corrosive, and mixing it with water releases heat.
